newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran closes candidate's campaign HQ as vote nears.
newsitem.headline: Iran closes candidate's campaign HQ as vote nears.

text.p: Iran's presidential hopefuls launched their final campaign efforts on Wednesday as authorities shut down the headquarters of a leading candidate for alleged violations of election laws.

Gholamhossein Rahbarpour, an official in charge of overseeing the campaigning, said Mohammad Khatami's Tehran headquarters were closed after officials determined that it was located in a state-owned building, the daily Kayhan said.
The Islamic republic's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei told Iranians the election on Friday would be fair. He strongly denied rumours about possible vote-rigging.
"Rumours that there will be cheating in the election have been spread by enemies," Khamenei said in a speech carried by state-run Tehran radio.
Khamenei was referring to rumours that officials might use their influence to help conservative Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, widely tipped to win, who is backed by key clerical groups.
"Personally, I won't allow the election to be unhealthy. The president will be a legal one," he said, adding that authorities were determined to ensure the poll's fairness.

Khamenei said a large turnout in the election would be "a smack in the mouth of the enemy" and urged voters to pick the most qualified of the four candidates allowed to run by the powerful Guardian Council which rejected 234 others.

Analysts said similar remarks by Khamenei in the past weeks had prompted clerics and hardline and conservative politicians to redouble efforts in support of Nateq-Nouri and against his rival Khatami who is backed by centrists and left-wing Islamists. Both men are Shi'ite Moslem clergymen.
Khatami, who enjoys wide support among women, intellectuals and the young, has come under mounting pressure in the campaign from Nateq-Nouri's backers for his relatively liberal views.
Khatami's headquarters were in violation of election laws banning the use of state funds and facilities for political campaigns, the newspaper Kayhan quoted Rahbarpour as saying.
He said the building was owned by Tehran's municipality, which is headed by the capital's pro-Khatami mayor, but did not say under what terms the candidate was using the offices.

Authorities also cancelled a campaign rally for Khatami and police turned back without explanation people arriving for the rally at a sports stadium west of Tehran. A staff member at the pro-Khatami daily Salam told Reuters the interior ministry had ruled that no election rallies would be allowed at sports arenas.
Both Khatami and Nateq-Nouri said in a televised debate they would aim to bring about the departure of U.S. forces from the oil-rich Gulf.
The presidency is Iran's highest elective office but second in authority to the supreme leader who has absolute power over all state institutions.
Campaigning ends at 8 a.m. (0330 GMT) on Thursday, allowing 24 hours for rest and reflection before voting on Friday.

Election officials and President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, who must step down in August after two consecutive four-year terms in office, have warned against violations and 280 people have been arrested for unspecified offences in the capital.
Rafsanjani has cautioned government officials against abusing their position to influence the election and said vote-rigging would be an unforgivable treason.

The Guardian Council, a powerful body of 12 clerics and lawyers which selected the four candidates on the basis of their belief in the Islamic system of government, said any poll violations must be countered without discrimination.
Some 33 million Iranians aged 15 and over can vote.
